utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is the last day of August, and I would like first and foremost to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Coric. I also want to greet Mr. Coric. I welcome our Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer and his assistants, and everyone helping us. I would like the Registrar to move us to closed session for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now pursue the cross-examination in open session. I now give the floor to Mr. Stringer, whom I greet once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon again to you and Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, at the conclusion of the trial session last week, we were just starting to work on a group of documents from -- relating to the period of January 1993, in relation to the area of the municipality around Gornji Vakuf, so I want to continue with those questions today. I think when we left -- when we completed last week, we were looking at P00460, which was from October 1992, and which was a document of Colonel Siljeg. Now, you don't need to go to that document, General, because I've finished that. I'm going to move to the next one. But before I do, I want to recall some of your prior testimony in relation to the events that led up to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf in January. And this is your testimony on page 40580 of the transcript from 21st of May, 1999. General, you were talking about escalation and the rising tensions in Gornji Vakuf, and you made a reference to the -- you asserted that the ABiH had closed off or blocked some roads in the region, and this required the HVO commander, Mr. Tokic, to actually get an UNPROFOR escort to reach his headquarters. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't just about the roads but involved also all the elevations in and around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it's true, General, isn't it, that at the same time, early January 1993 at least, the HVO itself was cutting off roads or block -- blocking roads in the Gornji Vakuf area, and this also contributed to the rising tensions? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. I knew about these things earlier on when I was there as far as the BH Army actions were concerned. Of course it is quite possible that there was some form of HVO response. This is a cause-and-effect principle that we see at work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at the next document in your binder which is P01068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, just a minute. The Prosecutor is talking about the blocking off of roads. During the four last years we've talked about this almost every day, you know, this blocking of roads. It seems that according to some military experts, blocking off roads would be part of the active defence strategy. It seems -- I haven't checked this yet. However, in the American -- in the US military doctrine this is part and parcel of strategy. So when the HVO or the ABiH is blocking off a road, according to you is this a defensive action or is this an offensive action? Or maybe you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know. The blocking of roads, isolating the brigade commander and taking all the significant elevations and trig points in Gornji Vakuf, in my opinion, can only constitute an open active aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P01068, and it is from the 6th of January, 1993, a milinfosum of the British Battalion that was based in the area, and I'm going to take you to a couple parts of this. The first part is in the second paragraph, and it says that a CS from Gornji Vakuf was approaching an HVO check-point, and it gives it grid coordinate. When the HVO sentry fired his weapon in the air, the CS withdrew back to Gornji Vakuf. "Comment: There is an earthwork barrier at this check-point in order to force the Muslim population of Hare to travel to Prozor and not Gornji Vakuf. Obviously tensions are rising in the area, which is reflected by an HVO presence at the check-point." End of comment. Now, General, recognising that you weren't there at the time, did you subsequently find out when you did arrive that the HVO, as indicated here, had erected barriers, at least -- at least at this check-point in order to prevent the Muslim population from travelling into Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my previous assertion about what went on in Gornji Vakuf months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph continues on, and it says: At approximately 1500 hours, on Monday afternoon, the HVO raised an Ustasha flag in the town. The Muslims reacted, and a Bosnian army soldier attempted to remove the flag. An HVO policeman then fired at the Bosnian army soldier in question, resulting in a sharp rise in tensions in the town. And then it goes on to talk about how the commanders managed to defuse the situation. Now, we saw the same thing in Prozor, General. We don't need to go back to the exhibit, but it was P00608, the Markesic report from October talking about rising tensions in Prozor after the Croatian flag was raised there. Were you aware of this, General, that at least on this one occasion the Croatian flag or an Ustasha flag, whatever you want it call it, was raised by HVO soldiers in Gornji Vakuf and that this also contributed to the rising tensions there in advance of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that incident. In the English report and the Croatian, one should point out that the word "Ustasha" is under quotation marks, which is the difference between speaking and writing. One must point out that in both the Croatian report and the Croatian translation the word "Ustasha" is under quotation marks, suggesting that this is no real Ustasha flag but, rather, the authentic historical flag of the Croatian people. I do wish to point out that during the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina this flag was hoisted whenever there was any kind of political rally. The flags of the Muslim people, the crescent one, and the Croatian flag were often associated as a token of friendship and often seen together. I would not exactly call this a sign of rising tensions, because if there was a side over there that minded even the -- catching sight of the Croatian flag, then this would have constituted a problem for that group, because any tension arising from that would have been tantamount to imposing the will of one people on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. So you're suggesting that the raising of the Croatian people's flag in Gornji Vakuf was intended to be a token of friendship? Is that what you're suggesting to us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that during the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina there were dozens of places, and these locations were photographed and I can actually produce the photographs. The Croat's flags and the Bosniak's flags would be actually bound together by a single knot and shown around as a token of friendship between the two peoples. The flags were together, meaning the two peoples would stand united against any form of aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A new day in court has started and a new week, and maybe some of the things that the Bench has told you over and over again has faded. You are invited to answer the question. The answer -- the question was: Is it your point that this raising of a flag was a gesture of friendship, and it can be answered by yes or no, and you would much assist the Court if you stuck to that and would answer yes or no to a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me suggest, with the Court's permission, a third answer that you should consider, which is the fact that since you weren't there, you don't know whether the raising of the Croatian flag was offered as a token of friendship. So it's yes, no, or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't think this is a question that can possibly be answered. I can only tell you that it is an inherent right of the Croatian people to raise their flag. It is a right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And since you weren't there, General, and since you've told us you don't know, then you have no reason to challenge the conclusion of the writer of this report, the British Battalion, that in fact this incident resulted in a sharp rise in tensions in the town; correct? You're not in a position to dispute that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do dispute that particular inference. I dispute its very essence. The raising of a flag belonging to a sovereign people can -- you're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I will look at this document but from another angle. We've already seen this document, it's no surprise to us, but as the trial is advancing, any reasonable trier of fact starts to see things more and more clearly. So the British Battalion is observing what is happening on the field and is reporting this so-called flag incident. We've heard some witnesses from UNPROFOR who told us that before arriving on the field they were trained, and they were given information on the situation at hand. So they weren't coming without any knowledge. They had been told about the ins and outs of the situation. At least this is what witnesses told us. And when reading this report, I note that at first this is a very factual report giving the facts. In this report there is no mention that this incident might, and I say might, might be in line with what the HVO is doing or would be doing if it was undertaken a joint criminal enterprise. If there had been an enterprise, you create an incident, you raise the flag. Because of this you get a reaction from the Muslims, and that gives you an excuse to launch some kind of military action. However, I have noted that in a number of UNPROFOR reports there is a paragraph on comments, but here I see no analysis of the situation. Thus in July [as interpreted] it seems that an incident occurred, but it seems to be an isolated incident. Now, please, could you tell us, as far as you're concerned, whether you think what happened in Gornji Vakuf was an isolated incident or whether this illustrates an incident that does not date back to January 1993 but which -- whose roots can be found in 1992 or even earlier in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, based on what I just said, the flags were regular during the elections. The peoples had their flags. I don't see how the raising of any of these flags should bother any of the other sides. That means there is something that isn't working properly with one of these other sides. Secondly, one of my tasks, both in 1992 and 1993, and during my time as commander, was to continually make possible +for weapons to go through and eventually reach the BH Army. You asked me what I was doing. One of my tasks was in a way to keep this secret, even without the soldiers knowing, to allow the weapons to go through and reach the BH Army. A lot of my energy was dedicated to that. For Merhamet's trucks, five or six of those, concealing the BH Army weapons, allowing them to pass through the positions held by my soldiers and me, and then those weapons were used against us the very next day. Any criminal enterprise would have stopped this sort of traffic all together. The HVO was strong enough to simply take those areas, round the whole thing off, and finish the whole story in October/November 1992. I will never justify myself before this court or any other court why I raised the Croatian flag in a country in which I was a member of a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking for justification. I was -- asked a very specific question, surgically precise, if I could say so. And the further -- you know, as we go on, I will be more and more specific. I really wanted to know whether this so-called flag incident was just an isolated incident or whether this was part of a plan at all. It's crystal clear. And you're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know there was no plan. This was a man who raised this flag. Another man reacted. What happened happened. There was no order to raise this flag. There was no speculation, Let's go and raise a flag here and then there will be a reaction by them. It was nothing like that. This was an isolated incident and tensions were allayed immediately because the commanders jumped in to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, a correction of the transcript. I think there is a mistake sneaking in there when the Honourable Judge's question was being interpreted. Page 9, line 22. It reads July as the month in which the incident happened that the Judge was asking a question about; whereas I think the Judge said the January incident, which the next paragraph records properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you, Mrs. Alaburic. I could have seen it myself, but when I put a question, I -- I'm always watching Mr. Praljak, and I can't see the screen at the same time. Professionally, I always want to look -- look at the person I'm talking to, and I can't check the screen at the same time, unfortunately. Thank you for -- counsel of Defence for creating the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the document next document in the binder is P01107. It's somewhat long. It's an order of Colonel Siljeg. We've seen it any number of times. I'm not going to ask you about it in great detail except for two parts. First of all, as we see in the preamble, and this is dated the 12th of January, 1993, he notes a deterioration in the relation between Croats and Muslims. He says the BH Army is attempting to take over key buildings in Gornji Vakuf which are under the control of the HVO, and given the incident that are present at all times, such as taking down the Croatian flag in the centre of town, arresting certain individuals on both sides, arrival of BH Army forces, et cetera, and the failure of civilian authorities to function, and in particular because of the attempt by the BH Army to eliminate the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, and then he issues this order. And my question, General, is -- is at the -- if you turn to the very end, we can -- I don't want to go through it. I don't want to take the time to go through this. He's talking about the attack forces, objectives, taskings of the various units, various brigades, use of artillery in paragraph 3, et cetera. And then in item 6 at the end of the document, he says: "Be prepared for combat immediately, which is to be started when I give the order." General, my question simply is whether we can call this a preparatory attack order or a preparatory combat order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is something that a commander must do. He must prepare, and then he says preparedness right now. The attack shall commence depending on my later order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on how the situation evolves. And then there were attempts --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave me the answer I was looking for, General. And the next question on this would be whether -- as I understand it, you arrived in this area, that is Prozor-Gornji Vakuf, if I can put it that way, on the -- late on the 15th or early on the 16th of January. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning of the 16th. I can't say really. That morning, before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After you arrived on the morning of the 16th of January, did you become aware at that time or subsequently that Siljeg had issued this preparatory combat order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he issued this, but on the 16th the fighting was already going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting started on the 16th, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is P01132, and we're going to take a moment to see what's being said on the other side. This is a document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 14th of January, 1993, and this is Mr. Hadzihasanovic writing to the Supreme Command, and he's talking about -- he says one of the most complex problems -- this is at the beginning: "One of the most complex problems the command corps has encountered since the corps' establishment to this day is the relation between ARBiH units and HVO units. Such relations culminated in the HVO's armed attack on Gornji Vakuf, resulting in huge material damage, the wounding of civilians," et cetera, and he goes on. And I want to move down to the bullet points that are at the end of the next paragraph. He first lays out a conclusion that the latest conflict is a well-thought out, planned policy, planned -- excuse me, well-thought out and planned activity on the part of HVO extremists and part of the HVO policy with the chief aim of an open conflict between the Croat and Muslim people. Now, this is Hadzihasanovic making this assessment and sending it to the Supreme Command of the ABiH. And in support of that conclusion he cites these facts, he says: "Civilians bodies of authorities, where the HDZ ostensibly won, are creating a state set-up in the state of so-called Herceg-Bosnia. Muslims as well as those who do not recognise the laws of so-called Herceg-Bosnia are being removed from the bodies of authority." He continues to say that: "Parallel bodies of authority within -- with the so-called HB's legislature are created in territories the HVO considers its own ..." Then skipping down, he continues by saying: "... the HVO units are confiscating weapons, equipment, foodstuffs, other means intended for the ARBiH, as well as that of humanitarian organisations." Now, General I'm not going to go back to the documents but, when we were talking about lead-up to the conflict in Prozor in 1992, we looked at a few of the documents related to the HVO's political takeover of Prozor municipality. Do you remember that? Do you remember the document we looked at where Dario Kordic signed on behalf of Mate Boban appointing people to the municipal HVO in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all my information the HVO did not take over political power in Prozor, but at meetings it shared the power and authority on the basis of the election results. That's my information when I was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I asked a different question which was whether you remember the document where Dario Kordic signed on behalf of Mate Boban appointing individuals to the municipal HVO. If you don't remember it, just tell me and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that document, and that's all I can tell you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And now what we see now a couple of months later in Gornji Vakuf is the same sort of reference or a reference to the same sort of activity, that is the appointment, the creation of parallel civilian or political authorities in these areas under HVO control. And the ABiH people here are concluding that that, in fact, is part of an HVO policy that's going to lead to open conflict between Croat and Muslim people. And isn't that indeed the case, that the establishment of these separate HVO bodies, parallel structures, is in large part what led to the military conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In Gornji Vakuf, complete power and authority -- or, rather, parallel authority was created by two people, Topcic or whatever the man's name was, and none of these points that Hadzihasanovic is setting out here is correct, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General - excuse me - the next exhibit is P01146, and this is one that we've seen a lot, and it's one of a series, and so let's just go through the series and then we'll talk about this issue of the -- the ultimatum or the position of the HVO in more detail. General, P01146 is a decision of the HVO HZ HB that was made or issued at its extraordinary session held on the 15th of January, 1993, in Mostar. And we see in this decision, and we've seen it many times already in this trial, the decision providing or directing that in Vance-Owen canton 3, 8, and 10, the HVO is -- well, the ABiH is going to be subordinated to the HVO, and in Vance-Owen cantons 1, 5, 9, the HVO is going to be subordinated to the ABiH, and in the documents to come, we'll see how this decision moved down the chain of command. Before we do that, General, this is the 15th of January, and you've told us that it was on the morning of the 15th of January, 1993, when you left Zagreb and made your way down to Mostar with the text that we find in this decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you're saying that the text of -- of what's in this decision --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th, before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And if I understand correctly, you're tell us that this text was text that was agreed upon in Zagreb in meetings that were held with you, Mr. Izetbegovic, Gojko Susak, and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in one or two meetings. They lasted for a day or two. I can't remember all the names, but Boban, Izetbegovic, Susak, yes, and some others, and I myself were there. I think I was at two meetings, not the whole of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I asked you about this last week, and you said that the agreement on this text was an oral agreement, that is, that Izetbegovic and his people did not sign off on a text. Rather, it was an oral agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. The document was compiled. It wasn't signed because the minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to make it public first. Bozo Rajic, he was the defence minister at the time. And I see no reason why it should be signed and initialed if the minister was going to make it public. Anyway, the text was drawn up, and they agreed upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So neither Boban nor Izetbegovic signed off on this text, but it's your testimony that it was going to be made public as an agreement nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the text was written, dovetailed, and handed over to the minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the defence minister, in fact. That's all. And I think he made it public on the 16th, and I think we've already seen the text of that during these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Coming back to this exhibit, P01146, this extraordinary session that was held on the 15th of January, 1993, in Mostar, were you present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the text of this decision, since it came from you, did you arrive in Mostar, give the text to the membership of the HVO HZ HB, and then they went in and had their extraordinary session? Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the author of the text. I took part in elaborating this document. So to be an author and to take part are two different things. I brought the text, that's true, and I handed it over to the gentlemen there, Mr. Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, so then my question is: After you handed the text over to them, is that when they went into this extraordinary session and passed this decision, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know how this decision came about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How it came about? Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No -- go ahead. I'm sorry, I didn't mean to cut you off. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when was meeting was. I don't know when they signed it. All I know is that I brought it as a finished decision, something that we were very happy to have put down on paper and that we would have reciprocity, and that this could stop any possible conflicts that arose from minor issues and that were more and more difficult to mitigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. The translation, Mr. Praljak, reads, "I don't know when they signed it," plural. I have only found one signature on the document. Why do you use the plural here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because a similar decision with very minor differences was signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic. So that's why I used the plural. I know of this decision. And then afterwards there were two orders, and we have seen those two orders here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Trechsel, the subsequent ones from Mr. Stojic and the others are coming so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have seen that. I have seen that. It will be interesting to know how they relate to each other, because at first look it seems a bit strange that one would have three identical, if they are identical, orders signed by different members of government. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I just wanted to take you to paragraph 1 of this. It says: "All units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which at this moment are stationed in provinces 3, 8 and 10, which have been declared Croatian provinces in the Geneva accords, shall be subordinated to the command of the Main Staff of the HVO armed forces." General, now, are you asserting that Alija Izetbegovic agreed to that language that Vance-Owen provinces 3, 8 and 10 had been declared Croatian provinces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that respect, an agreement had already been reached, and Mr. Izetbegovic agreed with it. And it was always emphasised that this decision, decision number four, was considered a provisional decision and would be in force until the final Geneva agreements were signed. So it didn't jump the gun in any way. It just made sense in one aspect. The fighting in Vakuf had already begun. I was asked to go down there and to try and assist the people to calm the situation down, and -- yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So -- and again when you talk about this agreement with Izetbegovic, you're talking about an oral agreement. You don't have President Izetbegovic's signature on this text anywhere, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, we have this decision here and the order, and it's signed by his minister in the government, Bozo Rajic. You asked me this ten times --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as if you think I'm stupid and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm actually asking you a different question which is, just to confirm for us, you do not have Alija Izetbegovic's signature on this text anywhere, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document as we follow this down the chain, P01140. And this is dated the same day, the 15th of January, 1993, and this is the document, General, that you referred to a moment ago that bears the signature of Bruno Stojic, head of the Defence Department. And he's issuing this order, which is pursuant to the HVO decision that we just looked at, and this is an order from the head of the Defence Department. We see it goes to the Main Staff of the HVO. It appears to be going to some command of the army of the -- command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, minister of defence, Bosnia-Herzegovina military police. In this one Mr. Stojic orders -- I'm not going to read it all but it is similar to, although not identical to, the text that we just were reading in the previous document. Ordering the establishment of direct contact with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the various Vance-Owen cantons in order to achieve an implementation of the decision that we just referred to. In number 2 he directs that the HVO is going to subordinate themselves to the command of the ABiH or leave the territory. And then he essentially says the same thing in paragraph 3. He says: "Members of the units of the armed forces of the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina ... who do not leave the territory of the province and do not wish to subordinate themselves to the relevant command shall be treated as members of paramilitary units who shall be disarmed and taken into custody." Now, General, would you agree with me that this reference to treating units as paramilitaries is not something that's found in the text of the original HVO decision that we looked at in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government is obviously making a decision, and the minister, on the basis of that government decision, is issuing an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He elaborates on the situation in such a way -- in a way that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question was a simple one. Can you agree with me that the reference to the paramilitary units here is not something that's contained in the original text that's found in the HVO decision? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have to take the original text of Bozo Rajic's to see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about the text that's in the HVO decision that we just talked about in the previous document, P01146.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And since the HVO decision, which is P01146, is the text that you brought from Zagreb, then this reference to paramilitary units is something new that Mr. Stojic added, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't say that I'd brought this document passed by the government but that I was bringing in a document that had been dovetailed and coordinated, and the original was published by Bozo Rajic. Now, it was you who said that I brought in this document issued by the government. I didn't. I brought the document that had been dovetailed, the one that was published by Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you're telling us something different now, General. A couple of minutes ago you told us that you carried the text to Mostar and that you handed it to Dr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic and the others. Now, are you changing your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I didn't say that the document that I brought was signed by Prlic. My logic is quite clear. I brought a document, and that document is the document that was published by Bozo Rajic. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- differences or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When did you give it to Bozo Rajic? This is new.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hand it to Bozo Rajic. Bozo Rajic received it from one of the participants at the meeting. Now, who gave it to him, whether it was Boban or Izetbegovic or both of them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. I want to skip down to paragraph 8 of this document where Bruno Stojic orders that: "The Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the HVO and the chief of the HVO military police administration shall be responsible to me for implementation of this order." Now, given that this in your view, General -- well, let me start over again. What this document purports to do, General, is to provide for the military implementation on the ground of a political agreement that you claim was reached; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And point 5 is particularly important, which speaks about the very proper conduct on the Croatian side. So I don't think you should skip that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph number 8, then, since we see military implementation on the ground of a political agreement, it's appropriate then that it would be the head of the Defence Department as the highest ranking -- or most direct civilian authority over the Main Staff to issue such a decision, isn't it? Civilian control over the military is what this shows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you correctly. I do apologise, but I'm not quite clear on what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at item number 8 where Bruno Stojic directs that the chief the Main Staff, who at the time was Brigadier Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the chief of the HVO Military Police Administration -- at that time it was Valentin Coric; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He holds them responsible to report to him on the implementation of this order. And so what this tells us, General, is that the head of the Defence Department had the authority to direct the military and the military police in matters involving implementation of political party -- or political policy or political agreements; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would follow quite obviously from item 8. After political agreements had been reached, it is quite obvious that in that respect, and looking at item 8, it follows that he has the right to ask that the Main Staff implement a political decision of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now and in fairness, you mentioned item 5 so I'll come back to it. I take it General, that you wanted to point out here that the Stojic order provides that there is to be proportionate representation in the command structures based upon the -- the proportion of soldiers on the front line; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And a consistent implementation of item 5, in view of the fact that the BH Army soldiers were more numerous and they were up at the front lines towards the Serbs, and if they were there they could take over command of the brigades in the operative zones and in the provinces in which allegedly the HVO had been given the right to command. So item 5 speaks about the very proper conduct. Let's have soldiers up at the front, and proportionate to the soldiers fighting the Army of Republika Srpska, in proportion you should take the command of the brigades in the operative zones. And I don't think you could have any more proper guidelines than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then the next -- the next step in this chain or in this process is the next document, General, P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. I would like to ask a question regarding number 6 here, where Mr. Stojic "forbids the engagement," I'm quoting, "of officers of the Army of BH who have influenced the breakdown of relations between the Croatian and Muslim people in their previous work." Mr. Praljak, what does that mean? What kind of officers are referred to there? Is it everyone who fought against the HVO, or is there a special criterion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't think that that's it. I don't know what it is exactly, but up until then there was just the conflict in Rama. They weren't fighting against the HVO up until that time, but then there was some information about some people like Paraga, for example, in Vakuf, and other people mentioned there. It was obvious looking at that that a certain number of people in the BH Army, some of them who had come from the Yugoslav People's Army, and we had every indication that in fact they were working within the frameworks of KOS, K-O-S, and that they were working to disrupt any agreement between the BH Army and the HVO and a Joint Command, that those people shouldn't become members of any joint commands or joint staff because they would do what in fact they succeeded in doing later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document is P01139, also dated the 15th of January, this one over the signature of Brigadier Petkovic, who was the chief of the HVO Main Staff. So here we see in the -- P01139. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is same date, 15 January 1993, and here Brigadier Petkovic makes a reference first to the decision of the HVO of the HZ HB, and with the document reference numbers we can -- we can confirm that he's referring here to the decision of the HVO HZ HB that we looked at a few minutes ago, P01146. And then he also makes a reference to the order of the chief of the Defence Department, and with that reference number we can see that he's referring to P01140, which is the Stojic order. So now he's taken the Stojic order, and pursuant to the Geneva agreements, he issues this order. And again, this is simply passing down the chain of command the terms or the provisions of the text that we've been talking about with the other documents on subordination of units based on which canton they were found in. And here we see in item 4 that the reference to the paramilitary units that appears in the Stojic order is repeated, then, in the order of General Petkovic, providing that: "Units which do not submit to the appropriate commands should leave the province where they do not belong. Otherwise, they will be treated as paramilitary units and disarmed." So item 8 then provides that this order is to be carried out by the 20th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is the question in relation to item 4? Am I here to answer your questions or do you plan to just read on? Item 4 reads: "Members of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the unnecessary microphones be switched off, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're about going to go on reading this document, then you hardly require my presence here, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm finish reading it, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, a bit of respect, please, for the Prosecutor as for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get through it as quickly as I can while being fair to you about the parts I'm going to ask you about. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, but what I'm trying to say is this: You're talking about paramilitaries units. No, that is not true. What this document is saying is that units, BH units or HVO units, that are not resubordinated again, that this will be another mirror image. If these units don't obey, be it HVO or BH Army units, such units will of course be considered as paramilitary units because they refuse to obey orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. This reference to paramilitaries, let's apply it, then, to the situation in Gornji Vakuf. As applied to the situation in Gornji Vakuf, since Gornji Vakuf was within Vance-Owen canton number 8, then the ABiH units present in Gornji Vakuf at this time would either have to submit to the command of the HVO there or they would have to leave. And if they didn't leave Gornji Vakuf, then they would be considered by the HVO to be paramilitaries. Isn't that a correct interpretation of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf the only unit that was there was the Jajce Brigade, and then Petkovic here again says in proportion to the number of soldiers on the battlefront, if in Gornji Vakuf there are more Muslim soldiers who will reach the line facing the Army of Republika Srpska, they will be getting greater proportion in command in the operation zones and brigades as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I'm asking you about the status of ABiH units in Gornji Vakuf that do not submit to the command of the HVO. And isn't it true that such units would be considered to be paramilitaries by the HVO after the 20th of April -- excuse me, 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That follows from the order and decision approved by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The decision again, and the decision approved by Alija Izetbegovic, this is text that was not the text that you handed over to Dr. Prlic in advance of the HVO meeting, right? Because we don't see that language about paramilitaries in the HVO decision, do we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm just trying to make sure we have an understanding on this. I brought along a document, I'm not sure what it looks like exactly, but the original is with Bozo Rajic. If you show me that document, I will tell you, to the best of my recollection, this is what was involved in, involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. We'll come to that. Now, I want to take you to the next exhibit, which is P01186. Now, General, this is the 18th of January, 1993. It's a couple of days before the 20 January deadline that is contained in the Petkovic order we just looked at, and this is a communication from Arif Pasalic, commander of the ABiH 4th Corps, and he's referring to -- we can tell by the reference number in the first sentence that he's referring to P01139, which is the -- the order we just looked at that was issued by General Petkovic, and he's talking about the establishment of the 4th Corps in November of 1992. He says -- he continues in paragraph 1 that throughout the time that the 4th Corps was established, he says: "Your staff and command of the operative zone did not express any interest in the questions, what command it was, its purpose and command structure." He goes on to say that on several occasions he'd been orally informed by the chairman of the Defence Department about it, but he reacted disparagingly and said, "What corps? Where is that corps?" Now, here we see, then, that he is writing to Petkovic, and in item 5 he says that: "I cannot carry out item 2 in your order due to the fact that the 4th Corps of the Bosnian Army and its units are not under your command regarding such decisions and their execution." I'm going to move back up to paragraph 3. He says: "I am informing you that I do recognise, I do recognise the HVO Main Staff as a superior command for coordination of activities on front lines and combat actions -- operations against the enemy, Chetniks and the remnants of the former JNA." So here -- and he continues on. He concludes by asking Petkovic to rescind his order. Here we have a direct statement from the ABiH side that this order coming from the HVO HZ HB through Stojic, Petkovic on subordination is not going to be respected or carried out by the ABiH; correct? They were not going to subordinate themselves to the HVO in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic had nothing to do with the Gornji Vakuf command. Secondly, Mr. Pasalic claims that he believes the Main Staff to be his superior in terms of coordination, which is precisely what Petkovic's and Stojic's document, the previous one, refers to. Thirdly, Petkovic says, "Start talks." That document marked the beginning of the talks between the commands of the HVO, the brigades, and the operation zones about how joint commands should be established in order to keep incidents, minor incidents, petty incidents, individual incidents, group incidents such as this one, from occurring, leaving the army commands in a very unpleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well -- yeah. Let's just continue on, then, with the events that follow, General. I'm going to skip ahead in the binder a little bit, and I'm going to take you to P01168. 1168. Because you say -- you've indicated that Pasalic was not -- well, you said he had nothing to do with the Gornji Vakuf command, so let's see if we can get more from the ABiH on their position.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said Pasalic did not command the BH Army in Vakuf. What could he have had to do with that? That's a different story altogether. The 4th Corps did not have any Gornji Vakuf units under its command. I would like to see some precision and let's not use diplomatic language when it comes to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Pasalic was based in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, do not talk to the Prosecutor asking for more accuracy. If you believe that the question is not well formulated or not specific enough, just ask him for specifications, but don't give any orders. He's just here to put questions to you. The question might be formulated a specific way. You might not like it. If you believe that in terms of military jargon it's not correct, well, just be more specific in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, what I said what Arif Pasalic was in command of Mr. Stringer changed slightly, and then I said that's not what I said. I didn't say he had no influence; I said the units in Gornji Vakuf were not under the command of Arif Pasalic, just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It might be that there was an interpretation issue. It's a bit nuanced. I read from the transcript. We were told initially that you said that Arif Pasalic had nothing to do with Gornji Vakuf. So let me try to clarify it. Pasalic was in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this order -- I'm not going to call it an ultimatum. You know the Prosecution's position is that this is in fact an ultimatum that was not carried out by the ABiH, and that's what resulted in the outbreak of conflict on or about the 20th of January. You know that's our position. For our discussion purposes, I'll refer to it as "this order." The fact is that this order on subordination not only applied in Prozor or Gornji Vakuf, it also applied in other parts such as Mostar. Isn't that true? It also was applied in Pasalic's area of responsibility down in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now if you'll go to P01168. This is the 16th of January, and this is Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the ABiH armed forces, and he's sending this out to commands of all the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to my learned friend, just in order to forestall any potential problems in Mr. Praljak's binder, maybe not. This document we only have page 1, 11 -- P1168. When I look at the English I see that it has page 2 and page 3, and then I'm looking at the English the translation shows who the signatory is. The original document in the Croatian does not have page 2. There is only one page. There seems to be an error there. Not in ours. Not in ours. It might be an error. It might be a photocopying error. There you go. I'm talking about ERN 8979, last four digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I can clarify it. What we have in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope there are no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't think there are. Well, in the original language version we have the page 8979, which counsel's just referred to, which ends at paragraph number 7 or item number 7, and then the following page that everyone should have is -- got some handwriting on it with the stamp -- it's got the stamp of Halilovic's signature and then handwriting under it. And if we look at the English translation, we see that it's indicated there that after Halilovic's signature on the stamp, then the rest of it is handwritten text and it's indicating the distribution of the document, the dates and the times that it was all sent out. So I think it's all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I mean, maybe I wasn't clear. I said in my binder it doesn't appear to be there. If General Praljak has it, if you have it, it's all right. He can go on discussing, but now that we've lost time on this document, I do have to say it doesn't tell me anything. This page 2, that is really page 2 of this document, but let's just let that rest. I don't think it matters right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I can give counsel the second page which has the stamp and the handwriting on it if you don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've got it. It's been given to us by our learned friends. I think that's a different thing, but if you say so, the ERN number is there, then perhaps that just might be the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, you've had a moment or two to look over the document. This is Halilovic sending out a command on relations with HVO HZ HB. It's an order, as he puts it, to commands of all the corps. Then he talks about the January 15th, how they were informed about the decision of the HVO HZ HB and the command of the unit commander of the Defence Department in Mostar, and he goes on to describe again this order or the document sent out on subordination of units in the various Vance-Owen cantons. And the first command is that the ABiH must not accept or act upon decisions of the HVO. He goes on ordering combat readiness be lifted. He orders, in paragraph 3, that within the zone of responsibility measures are to be taken to realise further cooperation with the HVO and to prevent any conflicts between HVO and ABiH army. He goes on to order that behaviour -- extreme behaviour has to be dealt with. In item 4 he talks -- he orders that they estimate the current situation and possible conflict situations in relation to HVO. Make a plan of measures for preventing them. So -- and all of this goes out. And then the indications in the handwritten part are that this is all -- this is sent out to Mostar, 16 January, Bihac, 1 K, I'm not sure what that is. So we've got pretty widespread distribution to the corps of an order that, although they're not to comply with this subordination order, they are to look for ways to cooperate and to avoid conflict. General, the fact is that as of 16 January 1993, the HVO really was the only party that was looking for conflict, if necessary, to enforce the terms of this decision on subordination. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. The decisions discussed the beginning of talks. Mr. Halilovic refuses to agree. He discards everything. Some days after that it was also discarded by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. On the 20th, he made it null and void, the order adopted by his own defence minister, and then the whole thing was placed on the back burner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just to stay with this let's look at the next exhibit which is dated the same day, 16 January 1993, 8.00 in the evening. P01162. We looked at this document during your earlier part of your cross-examination, General. This is a report of Colonel Siljeg to the Main Staff in Mostar, and at the very end -- well, bottom of page 2 of the English he says: "Tonight at Gornji Vakuf, Colonel Siljeg and Colonel Andric negotiated with BH Army representatives. There were no results. Unless there is an agreement, Gornji Vakuf, southern strongholds," and they're all listed there, "will be taken and our line strengthened." He says: "General Praljak sent them a message that they will be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ HB." Now, General, this is the 16th of January. We've got two things happening here. We've got Sefer Halilovic sending out an order to all his corps telling them to avoid conflict with the HVO but not to accept the decision on subordination. And on the same day, we've got General Praljak in the area informing the ABiH that they will be annihilated, they'll run over, however you want to call it, if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ HB. So I'll put my question to you again, General. As of the 16th of January, it was only the HVO that was looking for conflict, military conflict, and that it would do so if this decision on subordination was not accepted by the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. About the outbreak of clashes in Gornji Vakuf. The cause of the clashes and their continuation have nothing to do with what you're saying, that being any agreement that was reached and then annulled on how the joint commands of the BH Army should be established. The clashes in Gornji Vakuf broke out on the 11th, and they continued. Praljak did not say this. I didn't go there to impose any ultimatum on anyone. You will see later documents about making suggestions to Siljeg and Andric where they would say during the talks it had nothing to do with any ultimatum. It was only about them moving out of these strongholds around the town, the strongholds that they had taken for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when it says here that they'll be annihilated or overrun if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ HB, that's a reference to the decision on subordination that was issued by the HVO of the HZ HB; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm challenging the suggestion that I said this during those talks. Regardless of what Siljeg reported, that wasn't the line of action that I took during those talks. You will see the transcripts of those talks and the items discussed. It was no ultimatum stemming from the 15th and so on and so forth. What was discussed there was lifting the full blockade of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf and putting an end to the clashes in such a way that the BH Army didn't block the roads, which was, as I said in response to the question by Judge Antonetti, a classic act of military aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to stay with this specific issue a bit longer, Mr. President, but it appears to me it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's time for the break, so we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume our hearing, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, before the break we were talking about Gornji Vakuf and the events involving the order or decision on subordination that was issued by Mr. Stojic and the others, and I believe that we were looking at your -- I should say at the report of Colonel Siljeg in which he attributes to you a statement that was sent to the ABiH that they would be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ HB, and I understand that you deny having sent such a message. Now, we can move to the next exhibit, which is P01174, and this is the same date as the Siljeg report that we were just looking at, although this is a report on ABiH side from Dzemal Merdan and Enver Hadzihasanovic for the attention of the chiefs of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one's the 16th, and the other one's the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're right. You're right. Indeed P01174 is the 17th. And it makes reference to the commission for negotiations to resolve the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, and that's dated Gornji Vakuf, 16 January 1993, at 1845 hours. Now, General, you were present there during this period of time. Maybe not in Gornji Vakuf, but in the area. This commission that's referred to here, do you recall, General, that this was a commission at which ABiH and HVO representatives were talking, internationals were present in order to try to find a way to defuse the tensions in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Those were the demands -- or, rather, the recommendations that between the HVO and BH Army, along with the international community, the problem of the conflict in Gornji Vakuf should be resolved that began on the 11th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this report, Merdan and Hadzihasanovic are reporting about negotiations that occurred during the night of 15 to 16 January, it appears. In the second paragraph they say: "Around 1730 hours, the HVO representatives, Colonels Miro Andric and Zeljko Siljeg arrived. The preceding night, at around 2200 hours, they had gone to Prozor for consultations with General Slobodan Praljak." Now, is that correct, General, that in fact although you were not yet present in Gornji Vakuf, you were nonetheless consulting with Miro Andric and Colonel Siljeg in respect of negotiations and talks underway at the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They came to see me. I think it was the 16th, because the dates are a bit mixed up. On the 15th and 16th there was sporadic artillery fire, but I think it was the 16th at 2200, or whatever. Yes, they had consultations with me, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so is that correct if it indicates that you were in Prozor at 2200 hours on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now here Merdan and Hadzihasanovic are passing up -- or reporting on the various --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a little problem, probably something I didn't understand. This is referring to negotiations that happened on the 16th January. On the 16th January, I think, they say that around 1730 hours HVO representatives came, and that they said that the previous night they had consulted with Mr. Praljak. So either they get the dates wrong here, or Mr. Praljak got them wrong, because the previous day for the 16th is usually -- usually it's the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's safe to assume that in this case the 15th preceded the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No generalisation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wish I could shed more light on it. I don't know that the General can either. I think the General's indicated that to the best of his recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were in Prozor --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th. This must have been the 16th at 2200 hours. Now, what the date was then, it's on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Well, maybe if we can just at least focus not perhaps on the date of the document but on -- on the negotiations that took place after you met with Siljeg and Miro Andric here, because what's being reported is the HVO demands that they then brought back to the negotiations after meeting with you, and we can see them all on the document: "The HVO decision on the organisation of provinces is a temporary decision based on reciprocity." General, would you agree with me that the HVO decision referred to here is the decision of the HZ HB, HVO, emanating from Dr. Prlic and the government of the HVO that we looked at earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they received the decision of General Petkovic as far as the army's concerned. I think that one arrived, reached them. It's the decision which I still think was reciprocity and that all armies behave that way if they wish to cooperate with other armies. During World War II or after World War II or whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is this -- can we safely say that the reference to the HVO decision here is a reference to the decision on subordination that came from Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that it was probably -- well, Mr. Andric was a deputy, Mr. Petkovic's deputy, and the commander of the operative zone was Siljeg, so I believe that General Petkovic's decision reached them. That would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to read it all, but just moving down this we -- we see the various other items that are set out in this report, and the one I want to read next is: "Equality will be respected in all areas although the armed forces must be subordinated to the HVO, and their direct commander will be the HVO commander." So, General, is it safe to say that at least as of 10.00 p.m. on the 16th when you met with Siljeg and Andric, the HVO position was that the ABiH had to agree to the terms of the Petkovic order on subordination and that they must be subordinated to the HVO in those areas falling within Vance-Owen cantons 3, 8 and 10?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you there, along with respect for equality and reciprocity, and in the operative sense too. So the commander regulating everything -- well, the BH Army remained separate with its command. Its operative subordination as NATO functions, as UNPROFOR functioned in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so also all the armies function in this way. In the operational sense, they have one command. You can't do it better than that if you wish to avoid a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we see additional requirements of the HVO as reflected in this report, and one of which says, and this is again Merdan and Hadzihasanovic reporting about the HVO position, they say: "They demand a denial over the radio that they have torched mosques, massacred civilians and soldiers and killed civilians. It should also be added that a civilian was killed, the driver of an ambulance wounded, a soldier butchered, and another soldier killed as he was assisting in carrying the wounded soldier into the ambulance." And then it continues: "Unless these requirements are carried out, they shall not be responsible for any consequences of a refusal to meet these demands which are intended to lessen tension, halt the conflict, and introduce law and order in the area in which disturbances have emerged." So, General, all of these requirements of the HVO, these are all requirements that were issued by you in your meeting with Colonel Siljeg and Miro Andric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't correct. I talked about all these terms with two people. One was a deputy of the Main Staff. The other was a deputy of the main operative zone commander. And I agreed I had nothing against that because, among other things, propaganda was a major source or reason for bitterness among people, and so it's normal to ask for false propaganda to be refuted and denied, because when people hear things like that over the radio, they become very angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, would you agree with me, then -- well, let me suggest to you that in your meeting with Siljeg and Andric in advance of this negotiation with the ABiH, you were meeting with them in your capacity as someone sent by President Tudjman to calm the situation. You were an assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia and also a major-general in the Croatian army. So those were the positions that you held at the time of your meeting with Siljeg and Andric here; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent by President Tudjman and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I perform my duties, the ones you enumerated, and I agreed that what -- the terms here for calming the conflict were logical, taking them one by one, that there should be a mixed composition of policemen, proportionate, that there were to be no people with long-arms except for mixed patrols and so on and so forth. I had no criticisms to make, no objections to make with respect to what they would put before the BH Army in order to calm the situation down. Everything was correct, logical, proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, they consulted with you in advance and presented these demands to the ABiH after you approved of them. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they didn't need me to approve something or not approve it. I merely agreed. They were the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, was it your view at the time that demanding the ABiH subordinate itself to the HVO in Gornji Vakuf or be declared a paramilitary unit was a demand that would calm the situation there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you can see, that was not discussed here. It was a work in progress, a decision that needed time to be put into practice, whereas the situation in Gornji Vakuf was different, and this defines precisely what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's continue with the next passage after the one I just read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer. Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let me ask you again and again, both of you to slow down, please, and to have a pause between questions and answers. I would be very pleased if you could follow this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you just said that this was a work in progress, a decision that needed time to be put in practice, whereas the situation in Gornji Vakuf was different. So continuing with the text from where I left off, Merdan and Hadzihasanovic report: "This envisages that everything must be completed by tomorrow. If it is clear that these demands will not be carried out by tomorrow at around 2400 hours, or if there is no desire to carry them out, they will not wait for the following day." So the HVO was not only demanding that the ABiH subordinate itself to the HVO, but that it do so within a very short period of time here, 24 hours or less; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Gornji Vakuf was a completely isolated case. General Petkovic clearly states there: "Contact and begin negotiations for joint commands," and so on. Here it says: "Leave the trenches, the repeater station," and so on. So this is quite a different situation, and it's about something that we've discussed here umpteen times. The HVO here was engaged in active defence after what the BH Army had been doing for several months, that is to say, preparing to cut off all communications with Central Bosnia and placing HVO -- the HVO in Gornji Vakuf in a completely impossible military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, skipping down two paragraphs, they continue. They say: "Irrespective of their interpretation that these demands" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me to interrupt you, Mr. Stringer. I would like to add a question to the previous paragraph that you spoke about. There in the last two sentences they speak of borders: "The borders are closed, and the army is already prepared to move, and the borders will not be opened," et cetera. Which borders, according to you, does this refer to, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no absolutely no idea, Judge Trechsel, what borders this refers to and what Hadzihasanovic is referring to there. There were no borders. I assume he means the border between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, which army is ready to move, I have no idea once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm raising it because normally the limits of municipalities are not called borders, and therefore, your point that this is limited to Gornji Vakuf is a bit weakened, I think. If the word for borders in Croatia would be state borders also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, that's precisely what I said. The only border would be the border between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know what Hadzihasanovic is alluding to here, what he has in mind. I have no idea what borders he means here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, skipping down to the third paragraph from the end, they're reporting that: "Irrespective of their interpretation that these demands do not represent an ultimatum but a categorical position, I consider the demand an ultimatum and believe they are prepared to use force if we do not accept their demands, since they have already grouped their forces from the direction of Prozor and have carried out preparatory combat activities on this axis." Now, General, the preparatory combat activities referred to here, would that be a result of the preparatory combat order of Colonel Siljeg, P01107, that we looked at a few minutes ago that was issued on the 12th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, or partially. Mr. Siljeg envisaged a broader plan of action over there. However, in talking to me -- or talks between myself and them, the situation in Bugojno was completely calm. It had been quelled. So there that broad plan had nothing to do with anything here. Bugojno was quite calm, negotiations were underway of some kind. As I say, the situation was calm in Bugojno, and it was just a matter of the Gornji Vakuf situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then, in Gornji Vakuf at the very least, wasn't the HVO preparing for combat activities in the event that the ABiH did not accept these demands on subordination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, there were no demands for resubordination. Here it was exclusively a question of the fact that the BH Army had taken control of all the elevations, and we've been saying this for 50 times now. Let's be quite clear. The HVO had the right to resolve an unfavourable military situation of this kind by threat. And there's a categorical position taken here. It says dig in the trenches. Let's pull the units out of the town, and so on and so forth. So let me tell you my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I'm going to ask you more questions on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Stringer, but on page 46, line 19, the answer that General Praljak gave was not recorded as General Praljak said, loud and clear. It was a response to your question whether -- of whether the HVO was preparing for military activities if the BiH were not to accept the demands for subordination. Now, can you repeat your answer. You started by saying, "Mr. Stringer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The conflicts began on the 11th of January. So they had nothing to do -- the isolated situation in Gornji Vakuf had nothing to do with this text that Mr. Stringer says is an ultimatum, whereas I claim that it is a very honest approach to what was agreed with Alija Izetbegovic, a very proper approach to setting up two armies which wished to fight together. Everything else -- well, the 11th. This arrived on the 15th or the 16th of January, and we're dealing with the situation in Gornji Vakuf as it was. And we've discussed this with various witnesses, and we'll continue discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, the fact is that despite what you're telling us here, the report of Dzemal Merdan and Enver Hadzihasanovic here clearly indicates that the subordination is among the demands that are being issued by the HVO. Isn't that true? And this is perfectly consistent with the other orders we've seen coming from the HVO HZ HB, Stojic, Petkovic, right down the chain of command. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The decision here speaks about the establishment of the provinces. It says it's provisional, temporary, and not important for this meeting. And then it says if there are changes in the Geneva agreement, the Croats will adhere to that, but the demand of the HVO vis-a-vis the BH Army is precisely as follows: The specific demand related to the positions of the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf, which were aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit on this point, which is P01163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a follow-up question. I haven't taken the floor for about an hour, and I follow very carefully the questions and your answers, and I'm trying to see clearly through all this, and I have to confess that I do not see very clearly in all this. There is a document, the Prosecutor has mentioned it -- well, first of all, we've seen all those documents before. Those documents have been looked into through various witnesses, hence the need to see this very clearly now. We have a first document, P1107. On the 12th of January, 1993, Colonel Siljeg prepares an action on Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, and in this order the objective is to take control of roads and perhaps also of towns since Gornji Vakuf is mentioned. So the order is rather detailed, but I can also see that in this order there is no starting point for the action. In other words, we do not know whether the order was executed or not. And then we have the last document showed by the Prosecutor, and he looked into this document at length. It's P1174 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1147"], and as far as I'm concerned, I believe this document is very interesting, because from the outset, in the first paragraph, it states that during the night from the 15th to the 16th of January, there were artillery fire, but a reason is also given to that, namely, because the troop movement of the ABiH towards Crni Vrh, point 1303 had been detected. And this document coming from the ABiH states that they had moved themselves, that the movement had been detected, hence artillery fires.
