And the Prosecutor, but that's his case, linked the ultimatum of the 15th of January based on the document issued by Mr. Prlic, links this to those events. Any reasonable Judge could ask himself whether those events are all linked between each other or whether there is no concomitance of several events. In the last document you do play a role, because it is stated in this document. In other words, in this document it says that Miro Andric and Siljeg came to see you in Prozor. And then thereafter, they meet with the ABiH, which will lead to Merdan's report, and during this meet the HVO position is clearly defined, and it is detailed very clearly. And Colonel Merdan makes an assessment of the situation. We don't know whether it's Merdan or Hadzihasanovic, because we can assume -- but we can assume that it was Merdan who was cosigned by Hadzihasanovic. Merdan makes an assessment of the situation by stating that the HVO had come to express a position, but as far as Merdan is concerned, it's an ultimatum, and according to him, this would mean that should the conditions of the HVO not be met or executed, the HVO could attack because they have put all their forces together within Prozor. So what I'm interested in is the fact that you were in Prozor. We have seen it already last week. Your task was to be an advisor, but -- that's the first theory, but we could also think that you are managing all this, that you are preparing all this, and that you are doing that from Prozor. So I'm faced with two options. You are pulling the strings. You are preparing everything. You are sending your associates to meet with Merdan and to explain what you want or what your demands are, and they have to be met, or the other option is that you are in Prozor to try to defuse the tension given the events of Gornji Vakuf, and in that case there is no link between the events in Gornji Vakuf, the ultimatum, and -- well, basically that is what I've tried to summarise here. I have not formed an opinion yet, because everything is very complex, but I would like to know what is your point of view, and I would like to know whether -- (A), whether you were pulling the strings; and (B), whether, if it's not the case, whether there was not a concomitance of events which means that the Prosecutor could feel that this was an ultimatum. My apologies for being very long, but since last week I said that I had to be very cautious because we in the heart of what is at stake here, namely, your responsibility. I have to put on the table, as it were, all the documents, all the hypotheses, and to ask for your point of view, since I have not really formed an opinion yet, as I said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, whatever the case may be, on the 15th of January, 1993, the documents issued by Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic cannot -- because it must have been sometime that evening or late in the evening, that cannot have anything to do with the BH Army moving its units towards Crni Vrh. That is entirely impossible. Certainly that document saw the light of public day and the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 16th when Bozo Rajic's document came. That's number one. Number two, the clashes started on the 11th for an entirely different set of reasons. In this limited area of Gornji Vakuf, it had nothing to do with that. Number three, I was not the one who orchestrated this. I was merely an advisor. I am saying before this Trial Chamber this: I approved -- or, rather, I agreed, not in terms of actually granting approval, but during talks I agreed with Mr. Andric's and Mr. Siljeg's explanation to the effect that the situation faced by the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, having taken the elevations and blocked the roads to Bugojno and to Prozor, left it virtually cut off from any and all forms of communication. They had the right to deal with the situation by military action. Again, I agreed that this situation that the HVO had been made to face, starting with October, November 1992, December 1992, because those talks with the BH Army did not commence then, these two men, even earlier on when I was in the area, I sent them to conduct talks with the English over in -- and over in Gornji Vakuf several times to tell them about the situation, draw their attention to the behaviour of the BH Army to make it clear that that was not allowed and that there would have to be a response sooner or later. Again, I agreed with that. I agreed the HVO had the right to use military means to lift the blockade of their positions in Gornji Vakuf, get the BH Army off all the elevations in town, the two principal ones stated here, the repeater, Krc and so on and so forth. Everything that we've shown already here, but also that Bugojno had to be left in peace and that as soon as this limited operation was completed there would be no entering Gornji Vakuf, no conquering anything, no nothing. Proposals were made to the BH Army to keep this from happening. They were told to leave those positions of their own accord, to close the trenches, to make a joint military position, to move all the soldiers out of town and leave the town free of unarmed -- free of armed men. I agreed with that, Your Honours, and whatever the responsibility is that is at stake, I'm still saying that any army in that situation would do the same, made to face the same situation that the HVO was made to face by the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf. It's something that we call active defence in military-speak. As soon as this was done I got in touch with General Petkovic, who was in Geneva on the 20th. The orders came for the cease-fire and then the trenches were closing and everything else, and then there was nothing there would be unclear about my role, and I'm speaking publicly about exactly what my role was. So on the 23rd I managed, based on orders that came up there, to stop. And mind you, it's not easy to stop an army. The army had suffered great losses, as you've seen, to the effect that there would be no entering Vakuf, that the operation must stop, and that the agreement that had been signed now had to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Your answer, your very comprehensive answer, does somewhat meet my -- what I had -- what I was wondering, but my fellow Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A mere technical matter. On page 48, line 24, the document referred to by the President is P1147, whereas in fact he said and meant P01174. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: One last question on this document, General, that I should have asked you earlier. In the second paragraph here where they're writing about the discussion with Miro Andric and Zeljko Siljeg at the negotiations, they say that at the negotiations they, that's Andric and Siljeg, they were accompanied by Mr. Ivica Lucic, Ivica Lucic, from the information bureau of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, just for the record, is that a reference to Mr. Lucic who was the head of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly not because I didn't see him over there. I don't know who they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. To stay with this negotiation but to move on to the next exhibit, General, in the binder, P01163. And this is again another one of the milinfos from the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. The last question and answer, you said whether Ivica Lucic was the SIS chief. Mr. Praljak says no, but he would have seen him. I'm not aware that Mr. Praljak was present at the meeting that is at issue here. As I read this text, they say that Ivica Lucic was accompanying Miro Andric and Zeljko Siljeg when they came to -- to talk to them, but Mr. Praljak was not there, as I interpret this document. So how can you say that it is impossible that Mr. Lucic was there, Mr. Praljak? Wasn't there an error in your conception of the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I did not see Mr. Ivica Lucic over there. That is why I assumed that he didn't actually attend these talks. It is stated here specifically that there was a man who misrepresented himself there or made a false introduction. That's one thing. And thirdly, there were several men called Ivica Lucic. So my answer, for my part, was in fact quite specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It was specific, but it's not logical. How does it make -- how can you say, "I did not see him," when you were not there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about the meeting. I'm talking about the preparation for those talks, not at the meeting that I didn't attend, just that I didn't see Ivica Lucic, and probably he would have got in touch. I was talking about the probabilities -- the certainty that I didn't see him in Rama and then the probability that he didn't go to attend any meeting. And thirdly, they say this is the false representation or misrepresentation, that someone falsely introduced himself and they hadn't found out before the end of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, that's a mere assumption of yours. You cannot say this with certainty as you have pretended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I had looked at this document, and this is what I understood, and if I'm wrong, please correct me. I accept to be corrected whenever I make mistakes, of course. You -- in Prozor you meet Miro Andric and Siljeg. That's absolutely sure, because it's written down. You meet them around 10.00 p.m. the might before. So it must have been on January 16th. So you, Praljak, meet Siljeg and Andric. Then the next day, on January 17th, those two meet Merdan, but in addition, there's another person who says that he is Mirko Radic, and Merdan, after the meeting, discovers that in fact it is Ivica Lucic. Two conclusions can be drawn. First, when you met them at 10.00 p.m., maybe you also met Lucic. Or second conclusion, at the meeting on the next day, Lucic came to that meeting, even though he wasn't with you the day before, and pretends to be Radic. Now, maybe there are other assumptions possible, other hypotheses possible. At least there you have two. What is your take on these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say the Ivo Lucic, who headed the SIS, I didn't see him. The talk here is about Ivica Lucic from the information bureau. I have no idea about the existence of such a person. I'll refrain from everything else, because as Judge Trechsel suggests, I do not have absolute certainty. I wasn't at that meeting. I did not see Ivo Lucic, the one from the SIS, in the area at the time. There's another man over there, I think, whose name was Ivica Lucic. I'm sure in fact. I can't remember off the bat what that man was doing there. There.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, just let me ask one last question on that. Even though you weren't present at the negotiations, to your knowledge, did Mr. Lucic, the head of SIS, participate in negotiations at this commission on Gornji Vakuf? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to any information that I had, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now, the next exhibit is the British Battalion milinfosum from the 16th of January, 1993, P01163. General, I want to refer you to page 4 at the top of your version in Croatian. And the English is on page 3, starting at the middle of the page and it says here under paragraph E: "Colonel Andreivitich, the HVO ops zone commander, read the following message from his commander, a general in Mostar." Now, this is again in reference to the negotiations that are taking place at the commission. General, I'm going to put this to you that the Andreivitich that's referred to here by the British Battalion is actually Mr. Andric, but let's read the quote, the message that's contained in this. "At the Geneva conference it was agreed that all provinces would be administrated by the leading ethnic group, in this area the Croats. The HVO and Croats fully attend to abide by this agreement." And then it continues on to say that: "The HVO formally requests ABiH units to return to their normal locations, withdraw the units from Jajce ... in return, the Croats and the HVO guarantee nothing will happen to the Muslim population unless those suspected of, or accused of war crimes. The Muslim population will be given full equality, but the BiH must be subordinate to the HVO." It goes on to say: "All troops must leave, fill in the trenches, dismantle the barricades." Continuing down toward the bottom of the English version, page 3: "The Bosnian media is to report the following in its bulletins, a list of demands that it should be reported that the HVO shelled no one, shot no one, and did not burn any houses, and that all these actions were carried out by the Muslims. With immediate effect, the land border with Croatia is closed."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then it makes reference to two HVO brigades in Prozor, supported by tanks and artillery, ready to advance on Gornji Vakuf: "You will have until tomorrow to agree to all demands and put them into action or face the consequences. You are to send your reply via UNPROFOR. Comment: BH have stated that they cannot agree to all the demands. The HVO do not appear to be willing to negotiate their demands. Therefore an escalation seems inevitable." Now, General, this statement here of the HVO on its demands, this text is in fact the position of the HVO that was approved by you in your consultations with Siljeg and Andric. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion here is about -- well, first of all, the person writing this document can't recall the fact that Andric's name is not Andrejevic and Prija [phoen] is not Prijic. And by the way, this was all outside the UNPROFOR mandate, any observations they made, dispatching things like these they find it impossible to differentiate what Judge Antonetti believes they weren't properly trained and their reports are entirely deficient. Mr. Merdan conveyed relatively well what they'd asked for. It -- there's no need to -- I don't know. If that's what it says, then, well, why would I comment what this report says? It was copied with quite a number of errors. What two brigades at Rama? Based on just what do they see that, and who says they can close down the border with Croatia? Some commander in Vakuf. All these are things that -- well, they're just stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's one of the points, isn't it, General, that you're the only person in the area on the Croat side who has the authority to talk about closing land borders with the Republic of Croatia. Isn't that true? I mean, you're the only person that would have the authority to issue such a demand. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely incorrect. Based on what are you saying that, that an assistant defence minister can close down the borders of the Republic of Croatia. That is nonsense, inaccurate. Just to caught this short, entirely inaccurate. False. Absurd if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually there is a high degree of consistency between this report of the British Battalion and the report of Merdan and Hadzihasanovic that we've just been looking at, and the fact is, General, that both of these documents accurately set out the HVO position on Gornji Vakuf. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan's position is approximately accurate, except he believes this to be an ultimatum, and it wasn't an ultimatum. It was just a very categorical position as -- as he claims he had been told. I would not like to comment on this document, because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move on then. The next exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this document is of importance, because it does coincide with documents we've seen and it does talk about documents we have seen. And you're right, of course, there are some mistakes like Andric or Andrejevic, and so forth and so on, but still, the document says the following. We don't know what sources are used, maybe it's from observations, but in the document it is stated that two brigades are in Prozor, and I wondered immediately which brigades were mentioned. The Prozor Brigade, and maybe people from Ljubuski, those who were supposed to come. So that then we would have two brigades. And in this document there's also mention of tanks. But this document states that the forces are ready for action, and in the document they add that - we don't know where they got the information - they add that the borders with Croatia are closed. We do not know where they obtained the information, but that is what is stated. And the comment is very interesting, because according to the British Battalion, an escalation of the conflict seems inevitable. This is what is stated. We would like to know exactly what their sources are, where they got their sources for a number of facts, but as far as their assessment is concerned, it's obvious it -- they are sure there will be a conflict. Of course, you had no knowledge of this document at the time. So what can you say about this conclusion that they draw, the fact that conflict was now inevitable? Are they right? Are they wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, they're talking here about the inevitable conflict, about the positions of the BH Army and moving the units towards here or towards there. Clashes would break out. They were right. And I said that a number of times. The HVO had the right to take action, having very fairly made proposals as to how the conflict might be avoided. Given the fact that the BH Army not only refused to withdraw from those hills whereby they were blocking the HVO, but also move their units towards Crni Vrh, the clashes were inevitable. Look at page 2 of the English -- or, rather, the Croatian. What big weapon was it that the HVO had? Look at the number of Croats killed in the clashes up to that point. HVO eight, BH Army three, and so on and so forth. Wounded, HVO 20, BH Army 0. That tells you who was attacking whom and who was facing what kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P01194. Just a brief question. We've already touched on this. This is a report of the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's under seal, Mr. President, so I don't think it can be shown on the monitors outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Page 3. General, for you this is going to be under paragraph 3, "Situation in Mostar and Jablanica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "According to the Malaga Tactical Force in the zones of Mostar and Jablanica, there has also been an ultimatum from the HVO to the Muslims. While the deadline set by the HVO for Mostar seems to be the 20th, it is not clear whether any time limit has been fixed for the withdrawal of Muslim forces from Jablanica." So, General, this just confirms what you told us a little while ago, that this order or decision on subordination that was to come into effect on the 20th did not just apply in the Gornji Vakuf area, but it was intended to apply throughout, at least, the Mostar and Jablanica areas as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in Gornji Vakuf. Nothing to do with Gornji Vakuf. Talks are to be started. The HVO was prepared to make 20.000 of its soldiers available to the nine or ten brigades under the command of the BH. I believe that was the only way for the conflict to cease, the conflict that was later to erupt between the HVO and the BH Army. This reflects a deep misunderstanding of what it actually says. The only thing you should do is go back and re-read what it says. It's entirely fair. It's reciprocal. There's a mirror-image principle at work there, and it's in keeping with all the military standards according to which all the armies in the world operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's all contingent on the ABiH subordinating itself to HVO command in Vance-Owen cantons 3, 8, 10; correct? Whether it's Gornji Vakuf, Mostar, Jablanica, or elsewhere, if it's in Vance-Owen 3, 8 or 10, it's all conditioned upon ABiH subordination; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way you put it. I have nothing to add to what it says. It's very specific. On the 20th the whole thing was discarded. The solution to the problem in Gornji Vakuf was not to resubordinate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or indeed to chase the BH Army away from the area. It was just about them leaving the positions from which they were cutting off the HVO entirely and isolating the HVO. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The -- the next exhibit, General, is P01183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I was looking at the Spanish version, because I speak Spanish, and I was looking at the text and the message of the Spanish Battalion to its authorities issued. There's a lot of stamps. They are very well organised. You have the situation in Gornji Vakuf, and according to the ABiH and to the HVO, well, it looks like they're going to fight or to clash, but it is also said they strongly condemn this action, and they feel that everyone is responsible. So they're not taking sides either for the ABiH or for the HVO. They just realised that there is a situation on the ground. They are not stating who they feel is responsible for the situation, but as a precautionary measure they condemn any action that would be instigated as a result of the situation. Given the information that you had available, I was wondering whether when we talk about the Spanish Battalion could we say that they were strictly neutral or not, because, as you know, unfortunately they will be hit very severely by the death of one of their officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spanish Battalion had nothing to do with Gornji Vakuf, with the exception of generic stories saying nobody wanted war and all, that this was merely amounting to copying something that was already a copy, everybody pushing their own agenda and dispatching back to their own government or back to base anything at all just to make sure that something was being sent back in writing. The entire meaning of this was reflected in our requests, our requests that the UNPROFOR should have what is called a possibility or a mandate to maintain a peace that is once agreed. They didn't get that, and then instead of making sure humanitarian aid got through, they spent their days just moving around and writing reports. They did some good things, too, and if you ask me, SpaBat was very fair in the Mostar area when it came to the wounded, the transport-related issues. The relations were good as far as I was concerned. Anything we could do we did in that respect. They did their job. They wrote down what they wrote down and dispatched it to whoever, although that was not their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Praljak, that the question was not for you to describe how the Spanish Battalion acted, but it was only asked what is your view about their neutrality, and I believe that it is the crux of the matter, and it would be better for you not to describe or make certain comments about the Spanish Battalion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They told me that themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next one is P01183. This is now the 18th of January, 1993. This is a Paket communication that appears to have been issued or sent at about 1.30 in the afternoon, and it's Siljeg to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno. He's responding to their request for an evacuation, and he says: "We hereby inform you that given that this morning we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, there is heavy fighting going on over there ..." And then, General, just turn to the next exhibit. We'll talk about these, dated the same day, 18th of January. This is a document that I believe you have indicated someone signed on your behalf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please identify it for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, is this your order, P01202?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, I certainly didn't sign this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you if you signed it. I'm asking you if you issued the order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember with any certainty that I asked for five MGLs, but I would have nothing against having asked for this myself. And if I didn't, I can state that I wouldn't have minded asking this to be sent, and then perhaps somebody wrote this order and signed my name. So I consider this -- even if I didn't ask for this, I could have done. And then someone translated this request of mine into an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we're in Sanction. I just want to put up on the screen for a moment the transcript from your testimony on the 23rd of June, page 41882. Maybe it will refresh your memory on this. On that day, Judge Antonetti was looking at this document with you, and he asked you whether you issued the order, and you said: "Yes." And then you continued on to say: "... Your Honour, I didn't sign this document, just to make it clear. I said, Okay, fine, use my authority, and we'll ask for those three pieces to be returned by the Kralj Tomislav Brigade, but somebody else signed it." So again, General, apparently you're not willing -- your recollection is not as good when you answer my questions. It's better when you answer Judge Antonetti's questions. So does that help you remember that, in fact, this is your order, even though someone else signed it for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't question that I gave that answer to Judge Antonetti in response to his question. However -- now, whether in that number of documents and the facts, a request for three MGLs doesn't come under my recollections for me to be able to say 100 per cent yes, if my answer satisfies you. I can't write an order, but probably, most probably, highly likely I requested something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, these two documents together, P01183 and P01202, these pretty much confirm for us, don't they, that the HVO began combat operations against ABiH units in Gornji Vakuf on the 18th of January; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I don't know -- well, from the 11th of January onwards, along with the negotiations, the HVO started some actions, and I don't challenge that. I don't question that at all, because the BH Army units had taken Makljen, too. Now, what were they doing up on Makljen which is between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor? What were they doing there in the first place? But I'm not questioning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So we agree, then, that the HVO launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen as is indicated in the report or this document from Colonel Siljeg. We agree on that, then, don't we? On the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to an attack. No, we don't agree that it started this attack from scratch, just like that. You want to say that they were sleeping, they were quiet, and now you, the aggressors, want to attack. No, that's not true. I don't agree with that. There was an active defence in Gornji Vakuf, and you can go on about that until kingdom come. That's what the documents show and that's how it was. It is true that the HVO launched an active defence from 11 January onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And this active defence operation was launched because the ABiH refused to accept the decision, and the ultimatum of the HVO that the ABiH, among other things, subordinate its units to the HVO in this area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. That they should move away from the positions they had taken control of and that they should free the roads and engage in combat with the Army of Republika Srpska and to enable the commander of the brigade to come to his HQ in Vakuf rather than be escorted by UNPROFOR, that has nothing to do with the ultimatum in Vakuf, and I've repeated this for 28 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about some of the HVO units that were involved in the -- in the military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with channels. I suddenly get French, which I don't mind, but it's not the one that should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I wanted to know, between Tomislavgrad and Prozor, how many kilometres are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-five to Lipa, for instance. Tomislavgrad -- perhaps some 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. About 40 kilometres. The document that we have before us, which you have signed, please look at the seal or the stamp. First of all, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. It's not your signature. Now let's look at the stamp. There's a number 1, and it says: "North-west Operational Zone or area." I was wondering, in military terms, this document is asking for large-sized grenades. Any reasonable Judge could draw the conclusion that in Prozor you are heading the forward command post, and you are in charge of the entire operational zone, because the stamp is the number 1 stamp. So we carried this stamp 40 kilometres -- we travelled 40 kilometres, and so you are pulling the string. You are managing everything, and you go as far as to those details in order to have three rocket launchers. And as far as I could understand, you were there as an advisor to try and do some PR, but in fact, you do intervene in a military action. But I have to agree that it is not your signature. It might be someone who signed on your behalf, but I would like to know how you explain that this stamp, which represents this command structure, moved 40 kilometres to reach Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander, if that were me, wouldn't have asked for five MGLs. Quite obviously -- well, if we assume that I'm the commander, then the commander doesn't deal with three MGLs. They're not any rocket launchers. They're this other type of weapon with some small bombs that it releases, bomblets. I don't know -- well, since I know what I was doing there, somebody asked me, "Go on. Ask them." And then I probably called someone up and asked them to send this in, and then they wrote this order. I never wrote this order, but it is highly probable that I did request them to send them this. Now, who signed me, where the stamp came from, I don't know. It was the forward command post, so possibly it was Siljeg who took the stamp, or his staff took the stamp with them. It wasn't that somebody brought this particular stamp for that occasion from Tomislavgrad, but 40 kilometres with the road as it is, you'd have to drive for three or four hours to cover that distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will stop here, but I was wondering if there was no contradiction with the document where General Petkovic was making you play a role. But at the same time, we could draw the conclusion that you were not part of a command chain. You were an advisor, and you were bringing on board your knowledge, but with this document you are issuing orders, and this is what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I didn't sign this order, and I couldn't have issued an order. Well, only if my failure to act would create great evil did I violate some rules. This wasn't that case. Now, who wrote this, well, probably my request for these pieces to be sent, somebody probably took me up on that and wrote this. I didn't issue this order. I didn't sign it at that point in time, and I don't know which of General Petkovic's orders you're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. Could you please look at the document. You will see that at the top it says "18.01.93," it's handwritten, and it says 1900 hours. And in your language -- well, it was translated into English as "sent," and it says something like Pescano [phoen]. Is this your writing, your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it isn't. I don't have nice handwriting, but I certainly don't write like this. And it says the Main Staff of Mostar to the commander of the operative zone. I have no idea how anybody from the Main Staff of Mostar could send this to the commander, and then this person asking Tomislavgrad to do -- no. With the best will in the world --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document, I believe, is P01198. Just a quick question on this. I don't know that you would have seen this. It's a -- it's a report from Gornji Vakuf, 18th of January, by an Ivan Kraljevic, Assistant IDP Commander, and he's talking about the day's events in Gornji Vakuf, various combat activities, and in the third paragraph he says: "It was reported that two members of the Convicts Battalion were killed in the village of Uzricje today." Now, General, this is January of 19 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say "battalion" anywhere. It just says the convicts -- well, I've never seen this document, and I can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if the members of the Convicts Battalion, under the command of Mario Hrkac, fought as part of the -- the combat in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of them were under Hrkac and were up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And they would have come from Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document, and this relates also to units involved in the Gornji Vakuf operation, P03090. General, this is a report on the work of the HZ HB military police for the period January to June 1993. It's dated July 1993, over the signature of Valentin Coric. And, General, in your version if you turn to the Croatian version page ending with the numbers 6216, 6216.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's pages -- page 6 of the English, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for you, General, ends with 6216 of the ERN number. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we start with this document, perhaps it's time for the break. I think the General's indicated that he'd like to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. We can have a break now. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor. [In English] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Your Honour, before I begin, perhaps I should inform the Trial Chamber and the other Defence teams what I just informed Ms. Pinter about so that everyone knows about sort of the pace of what may be left. We're on our list seven, now, binder number seven, and I think that the way it's looking is there will be three more binders, and I think they're all going to be in the smaller-sized binders. Not the big fat ones but the smaller, so indicating a smaller number of documents, and after those three I think there is going to be a very small amount of just loose-end documents that I'm going to come back to, but my hope is that certainly by the end of this week we're very close to the end. Maybe that's too ambitious or unrealistic for me, but that's my -- that's my wish anyway. So we're sort of working our way through. I think there's going to be three more binders and then a little bit of loose ends and then we'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document here is P03090, which is this work on -- report on the work of the military police for the first -- first half of 1993. Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And are you at page 6216 of your version?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is page 6 of the English. And we don't need to get into this in depth, but this report describes the role and activities of military police units that were a part of the Gornji Vakuf operation. And I'm not going to read all of it, because we all have it in front of us. The fourth full paragraph on the English version says -- first it's talking about units. Well, it talks about the overall attack launched by newly arrived HVO units and HVO military police units. This is on the 18th of January at 0400 hours. Do you see that? It says: "On 18 January, 1990" --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question simply is this: General, it makes a reference to newly arrived units and HVO military police units. Are you able to tell us which HVO units arrived from elsewhere and participated in the operations on the 18th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I have seen some of Siljeg's orders here in this courtroom specifying how many men came and from where. I think that is indisputable. The documents that I've seen specified that, the number of men and where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So we agree, then, that there are HVO units that arrived in -- as -- that participated in the Gornji Vakuf action that came from other parts, although you can't remember which units. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've seen the same documents as you. I cannot agree to anything other than that's what the documents say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and the military police units here that arrived, the next paragraph says: "The military police units were commanded by the 1st Light Assault Battalion commander and Military Police 2nd Battalion commander." Do you know if Zlatan Mijo Jelic is one of those commanders that is referred to? Did he command military police units in the Gornji Vakuf operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And while the military police units were in the Gornji Vakuf theatre taking part in these combat operations, were they subordinated to the operative zone commander, Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. They talk about cooperation. I can't answer the question accurately, but I don't think there was any resubordination. At least I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because we've talked about this a number of times, about whether military police units would, for operational purposes, be subordinated to the operative zone command. You do recall that subject; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject was discussed in terms of me during my time as commander of the Main Staff, and the Light Assault Battalion of the police, those units, not the regular military police, but those police units were trained for military activity. Those were subordinated to me for a certain amount of time for specific missions in specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, for Gornji Vakuf, January 1993, you do not know who was in direct command of the HVO units that came into Gornji Vakuf and fought there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It says what it says. I'm unable to comment anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cooperation was established, and the commanders exercised command over their units --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the way specified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I was looking at this report from the military police. This is how I read the document: According to this document, the conflict started on January 7th. This is written in the document in black and white. It says that the local military police had 50 people and was reinforced with 92 members of the 2nd Battalion and by 40 members of the 1st Assault Battalion. If I add all this, I end up with 172 military policemen. Then after the fighting on January 11th it seems that another 99 members of the military police of the 2nd Battalion arrived as reinforcement, as well as 53 members of the 1st Light Assault Battalion. And when you add all this up, you end up with close to 300 military policemen fighting on the field, which is a huge number of policemen. Obviously the fighting was fierce. On January 18th, the fighting is still going on and will actually continue until about January 22nd. It's still going on on January 23rd and on January 24th. In the English version, on page 7, we see that 10 military policemen were killed and 63 wounded. A few months ago, maybe a few years ago, I was quite surprised at the number of casualties in the military units -- military police units, and here we have a confirmation of this. So it seems that there's fights, combat going on leading to a great number of people being killed or wounded. When reading this document, I note that sometimes the fighting starts at 4.00 a.m. Everything seems to be very organised. However, what's missing here is to know what happened exactly on January 7th. Why is it that so many military policemen were brought together in the field? I -- you know, I end up with 300 of them. It seems that it was a large-scale operation. Now, you were in Prozor. Were you aware of the presence of all these military policemen that were sent over there to end up being -- to end up being a force of 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of members of the battalions of the military police and the Light Assault Battalion participating in the fighting. I didn't know specifically about the numbers, but they didn't all arrive on the 7th. On the 11th, the severe clashes started, and then obviously, as it says, another 99 policemen came, and 33 members of the Light Assault Battalion. And then it goes on to say that all the prominent elevations around the town were being held by members of the BH Army. I think another thing that's noteworthy here is reinforcements came to form a ring around the BH Army positions being held surrounded by the HVO, who happened to be there at the beginning of the clashes. It's precisely what I've been saying throughout. The prominent elevations around the town were being held by the BH Army and the HVO was being surrounded, as well as the military police, in town when they found themselves there, and that's when the HVO began with these other data. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, on the 24th there are no further clashes. There is only talk here of the 23rd, when they launched another attack. On the 22nd, Siljeg and I agreed or, rather, we conveyed an order that had arrived for all activities to cease, all military activities, and that Vakuf was the -- no longer to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, you pre-empted my next question almost. I was trying to find out why there's such a high casualty list. The combat must have been fierce, but maybe it's because of the terrain also. You've told us that the ABiH had dug up trenches, almost bunkers, you know, and that they had to be captured, which makes plain why there's such a high casualty list. So was this a close combat? Why do we end up with so many killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 22nd I looked at some of the bunkers over near the -- over near the repeater and Krc, and I assure you they were awfully -- and I have shown photographs here, 20 years later, those same bunkers, those were fortifications that can hardly be seen anywhere else. To take that sort of thing would have taken an exceptional military feat, and that's why this resulted in an incredibly high number of wounded and killed. The bunkers took months to build at these prominent features and elevations. You saw those documents from later on. The commander walking around with UNPROFOR and then saying, We'll close this one and that one, and then they were saying no. There they stood up to him, they wouldn't be closing that, and it was a bit like that. So in terms of fortifications, this was done by the book. They were perfect excellent bunkers. There was very -- they were very difficult to take, and the fighting was obviously very severe but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taking a bunker is a very difficult thing, a fortified bunker like that. No mean feat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the transcript, page - just a minute - 74, line 11 to line 14. We see your question there following up on the reading of that document and your statement concludes: "This was written in the document black and white, and it starts with the fact that the conflict started on January the 7th." Nevertheless, that is not what the document states. Obviously this caused a problem with the interpretation. Before the beginning of the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf on the 7th, and we can't see the number there, of 1993, in Gornji Vakuf. The 7th of January is not when the conflict erupted. This is just for the transcript, for this to be verified. And then if we go on reading the text it shows that after the clashes broke out on the 11th of January, 1993, and so on and so forth. Since General Praljak's statement will be analysed in detail, we just want to make sure there are no discrepancies between his evidence and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you slow down, please. Thank you. Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction of the transcript. On page 76, lines 1 through 4, General Praljak spoke about who was being held surrounded by whom, and if I understood correctly, he said that the HVO was keeping the units -- or, rather, the members of the BH Army surrounded, and then those members of the BH Army were keeping the members of the HVO surrounded, which would imply that these were actually two rings, whereas the transcript reflects something entirely different. If you believe that to be relevant, perhaps we should ask the General to repeat this for our benefit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, did you actually say that the HVO was encircling members of the ABiH, but that they had already encircled members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why the HVO action was launched, because the BH Army had been keeping the HVO units and military police in town surrounded for a month, and then the units that were entering the fray formed the outer ring and were taking elevation by elevation in order to free the HVO from its isolation. That's what it says, and that's what I've been saying throughout. Not just me, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mrs. Alaburic. This cleared the situation. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to skip ahead to go to Exhibit P01293. Now, General, this does not appear to be a document with a date. It's a handwritten document from Geneva and from Brigadier Petkovic in Geneva. Do you recognise this document, or did you see it during roughly the period we've been talking about, the third week of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the document, but I knew that an order had arrived from General Petkovic. I think this is -- I think this document is in reference to the 23rd, possibly the 24th of January. Why? Because on the 23rd of January, that morning, having visited the wounded commander Andric in hospital near Prozor, in Rumboci, I left for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as indicated in item 3 of this document, then, Petkovic directed Colonel Siljeg to report urgently to you and to send a report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf directly. Do you recall what Siljeg was to report -- well, let me back up. When Siljeg's to urgently to Brada in Mostar, is that a reference to you, "Brada"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did Siljeg continue to report to you about the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that Siljeg would forward the report to me. It just says that he would be getting in touch with me. He would be sending a sitrep on Gornji Vakuf to the HVO Main Staff in this sentence, to get in touch with me and send a report. It's not to send a report to me but to get in touch with me, yes. That's true. Yes, and then -- well, then I will not go further into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was supposed to get in touch with you about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Despite the cease-fire that had been signed, the BH Army continued to stage acts of provocation. Siljeg was a commander surrounded on all sides by dead and wounded, and he was in command of that army. It was difficult for him to simply put an end to the attack, but an order had arrived from Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic. I was supposed to tell Siljeg, The orders have arrived, stop at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then related to this is the next exhibit, P01277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor seems to move quickly to another document. I would like to stay on this document that is coming from Mr. Petkovic. It is handwritten by Mr. Petkovic, and this document seems to be important, because it is written "Urgent" three times. As far as I can understand this document, Mr. Petkovic, from Geneva, is writing directly to Siljeg, asking him to stop all operations, and then he's asking him to contact you and then to draw a report. So this document is rather surprising. We could wonder whether General Petkovic had wind of what was going on, which would mean that he was not aware of what was going to happen. That's the one possibility. The other possibility is that he was aware of it and the international community said that it was unbearable and that everything had to be stopped, and that's the reason why he's sending this document. My question is the following: When did you get to know General Petkovic's position from Geneva? In other words, when did you hear that he wanted to stop everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I managed to go through Gojko Susak -- or, rather, his secretary, and get in touch with Geneva. I asked that orders be sent through on the cessation of all activity. It arrived. I think Mate Boban signed on the 19th, and Petkovic on the 20th. I don't believe Mr. Petkovic was privy to every single detail over in Geneva at the time. Orders arrived on the cessation. As you know, a military operation is not something you can put an end to just like that, blowing out a candle. On the 22nd, an agreement was drawn up in Gornji Vakuf, as far as I remember. Siljeg stopped the whole thing. What this is about, obviously, is that Siljeg was facing a far more difficult situation than Petkovic over in Geneva and everyone else. He was still facing all these provocations on the ground and cease-fire violations by the BH Army. Nevertheless, regardless of the fact that there was sniping activity still ongoing, as far as I remember, killing our lads, the operation needed to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that Mate Boban reached an agreement with the other side on the 19th, and the order comes on the 20th to stop all activity, and General Petkovic has sent this message so that everyone is aware of this, but in the previous document what do I notice? Well, I notice that on the 22nd of January, namely, two or three days later, at 4.00 a.m., an attack is launched against the Rincigav [phoen] village, and I don't understand. You say it's very difficult to hold a military operation, and you're right, but when orders are coming from Mate Boban, they are also coming from Geneva via Mr. Petkovic and, and Mr. Siljeg is also informed. I was wondering how it is possible that on the 22nd of January, at 4 a.m., this attack was launched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, Your Honours, the reason being the order had been sent to the other side too. You should bring those commanders here and ask them who was still attacking and what the response was. On the 23rd, obviously there was a small-scale action, no more than that. It was started and not finished. Perhaps it was provoked. It's not for me to say. But it is not possible to end a military operation on a five-minute notice. All the units are still on the ground. You need to tour the units. You need to inform everyone. Someone is in the middle of a combat operation. If you just put an abrupt stop to it, you face heavy losses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I do not want to put you in a difficult position, but you know the three-C rule, control, communication and command, and I'm sure you're aware of all the rules, which means that from the private up to the head of the military operation there must be communication. And if the order is coming from Geneva to stop all operations, I find it difficult to believe that on the 22nd of January some activities were still going on. So you give us an explanation and you say, and I'm sure you're right, that one would have to find out under which conditions and who attacked first. I agree with you. But you also have to agree with me that it took several days for the orders to reach the ground from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. You need to go to each and every position. We're talking about communication, communication between Geneva, Mostar, Siljeg, and each of the units on the ground. This was not the kind of communication that is not familiar to a modern-day army, unfortunately. I do know everything about the three golden rules in the military, but you know, there is army and army. The communications in that area were exceptionally poor. Poor. What am I saying. Every time there was some line of communication it was constantly disrupted by the other side, by the enemy, and that is the best I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I think that it was the pre-trial brief from the Prosecution where it says that a double game was played. You say one thing, and you do something else. General Petkovic could say, Do this, but then say, We all agree that we are going to do the opposite. What is your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My take on this, Your Honours, Judge Antonetti, is this: The HVO positions in Gornji Vakuf on the 22nd of January were such that I'm putting it to you that Gornji Vakuf could be taken in its entirety in a single day, but no, that was not the objective. I conveyed those orders staking my own authority on it despite the large number of dead and opposition from my soldiers who might as well have refused to fight the next day. They were professional soldiers having suffered large-scale casualties, and knowing that they were under attack, they would obey and still be there in the ranks tomorrow. That is a higher level of skill. If I may use foul language, they might just as well have told me to sod off, left the area all together and I couldn't have possibly done anything to them. This was not the US army, this was not the French army, a fully professional army where I had full control. These were people who ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to take you to the next exhibit now, which is P01278. This is one of the British Battalion milinfo documents dated 23 January 1993, and section 1 is about Vitez. Section 2 is about Kakanj, and then I want you to look at section 3 on Gornji Vakuf. Now, this is the report, Vakuf, and then we're going to move down to about halfway through this paragraph where first they say that they dropped off ICRC medical supplies at BiH and HVO medical posts in the town. Do you see that? And then it continues --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "Talks occurred between HVO and BiH and a truce agreed from 2318 hours and 241200 hours when further negotiations will take place. At 1635 hours the village of Bistrica came under rocket attack from an HVO" -- some form of weapon is indicated there, BM 21. "The houses in the village were reported to be burning fiercely. Company 1 Cheshire," this is a regiment of the British Battalion, I should add, "is keen to stress that this is definitely ethnic cleansing by Croats on a Muslim village. At 1910 hours, fighting was continuing within the town. There is no cease-fire being implemented by either side." Now, General, this is the 23rd of -- were you aware that Colonel Siljeg and HVO forces were engaged in ethnic cleansing of Muslim village Bistrica as is indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't accept that for the simple reason that ethnic cleansing cannot be carried out with a rocket attack. If the HVO units were in the village of Bistrica, then you can't shoot at that village with a multiple-barrel rocket launcher. And if you use a multiple-barrel rocket launcher, then houses cannot be aflame because that's not what that -- those weapons produce. So this is quite unclear militarily speaking, that you could use one charge of 12 rockets or 21 rockets, anti-infantry weaponry, to cause ethnic cleansing and to have houses burst into flame in this way. And that speaks of the level of knowledge that the person who compiled this has.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the damage from another source that you might consider to be more reliable. If you would turn to P01351. 1351. Now, this, General, is a report of Colonel Siljeg, report on situation in Gornji Vakuf on 28 January 1993. And he's reporting to the Presidency of the HVO of the HZ HB, the government of the HVO HZ HB Mostar, Defence Department, and the Main Staff. And I want to take you to page 3 of the English version, and this is where he's talking about a sub-commission that toured villages per requests and determine the situation in those sectors. This is a report of the commission on establishing the factual state of the occasion. Combat operations in these various areas. Now, the first village that's referred to here is a place called Uzricje, and it talks about persons taken away, persons who had been killed. There are references to houses being torched, and this continues for other villages as well, property that's looted, again imprisoned soldiers. I'm looking at page 5 now of the English. Killed civilians. This is in Duse. A total of 18 houses and sheds destroyed, 16 of which were torched. Trnovaca is the next village, number 3. Again, four houses destroyed, torched, looted. And this continues on. And then on page 7 of the English, there's a reference to Bistrica, which is the village we were just talking about in the previous document. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Bistrica. Bistrica is the most critical point it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "... and we have to calm it down on our side, and when a global solution is found, then we know what we shall do in Bistrica and in other places." And then -- first of all, General, recognising that you probably did not -- well, did you ever see this report of Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And these villages that he's reporting about, is -- do they appear, can you tell or do you know whether they appear to be Croat or Muslim villages? Or mixed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here exactly what it is, but you're not giving me enough time for me to read through this and to comment, nor do I know from this point in time how mixed they were, which is which. I can't comment really. This is a document that was signed by Mr. Siljeg on the 28th, and I had played my role a long time ago, and I described what that role was. I was no longer in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. It is a commission report. Obviously he's writing what he is setting out. Whether it's correct, how far it is correct, I don't know, I can't say, but quite obviously the commission has signed -- has described all this, everything that was destroyed, what was looted, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, that leads to my next -- excuse me, my next question, because we know that you were present in Gornji Vakuf at least from the 16th to the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was in Rama.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. You were in Prozor meeting with Siljeg and Miro Andric from the 16th. Did you stay in Prozor until the 23rd when you left?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left on the 23rd in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you never went to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did once. I did go to an elevation to the left of Gornji Vakuf, in the direction of Krc and the repeater station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so throughout this period of time, 16th to the 23rd of January, General, you were consulting with and, in fact, you were issuing orders to Colonel Siljeg, and then, as you say, you left. Now, are you claiming that by leaving the territory you're excused from any responsibility of what happened in Gornji Vakuf if, in fact, you were holding a command position there during the time of the 16th to the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't holding a command position, Mr. Stringer. I came with a specific assignment, and I told you what I did. I told you when I left, and I don't feel responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the fact is that Siljeg, Miro Andric, consulted with you about the HVO policy and its demands which were rejected. Conflict resulted. You think you bear no responsibility for what happened up there simply because you left on the 23rd of January?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that the conflict arose because, as you say, there was an ultimatum. That is not correct. Now, whether I should feel responsible or not responsible for having left on the 23rd, that's not correct either. It's not correct that I issued an order, and I'd like to ask Their Honours where I'm asked a question -- well, could you please establish whether I was in command. Now, if I answer the question, am I answering everything that the Prosecutor uttered earlier on. So please break up this question and ask, "Were you in command?" Then your next question. You're making five assertions and after five assertions you're asking one single question and I can't answer that question because it would mean that I answer in the affirmative to all your previous questions, which I don't agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll break it down and I'll put it to you this way. General, isn't it true that the documents we've been discussing today clearly show that you did hold a command position or you held command authority in respect of Gornji Vakuf even though you did not hold an official military rank or position in the HVO? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true, incorrect. None of the documents point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that you knew that in these various military operations Muslim houses were shelled, torched, burned, civilians were ethnically cleansed, as the British Battalion says, throughout that period, and that despite having this command authority, you did nothing to prevent it or to cause, order any investigation or prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you have just said that you are going to break down, but now you're really putting question over question, and in my mind I can see a whole network of which goes right and left and then on -- I think it will be good if you took it piece by piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, did you ever order an investigation or do anything to prevent the crime that were committed against Muslims in Gornji Vakuf during 16 to 23 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a function which would require me to order an investigation about what happened in Gornji Vakuf. And apart from that, Siljeg writes and says what happened in Gornji Vakuf. Now, apart from the fact that he says what happened in Gornji Vakuf, he doesn't say who the culprits are, who did what, when. This is an observation of the situation, the state of affairs, whereas an investigation comes after that. And it was his duty as commander of the operative zone, or, rather, of all the other structures dealing with this, the prosecutor, the civilian authorities, the police and so on and so forth. It's their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So I know you've said this before. We should just -- I want to come back to this. Your position, General, is that you and Siljeg, unless you actually know the name of a -- of a particular perpetrator, have no obligation to prevent or to order an investigation. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not what I said. You talked to Siljeg, and you resolved that with him. You're now dealing with my role in those events, and I've described that role in very precise terms. Siljeg here, within the frameworks of the commission and a good commander, is making an observation of the state of affairs. Afterwards, he will take the steps in his power to uncover the possible perpetrators of those acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. General, a few questions, probably for the rest of the day, on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which of course is looming largely in the context, in the background, when we discuss Gornji Vakuf. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before discussing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, I have a few questions. I'm still looking at the document. Colonel Siljeg is reporting, and he seems to be very frank about the facts that he has been told about in his report. As far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned, he mentions the case of Vlatko Rajic who abused and decapitated an invalid. Now he doesn't say whether he, Colonel Siljeg, actually reported this to the military or civilian prosecutor. Secondly, he's also talking about the case of Branko Sapina. We discovered that the brother of Branko Sapina was killed, and because of this Branko Sapina is going to separate two civilians from others and is going to kill them, you know, with a pistol in front of all the inhabitants. What did Siljeg do? Did he report this to the civilian or military prosecutor? Well, we don't know. But Colonel Siljeg does report a number of facts, facts that require some follow-up, and there might have been a follow-up, I don't know, but this is the situation as it stands. According to you, did Colonel Siljeg behave properly? Should he have drafted a report saying, "I will report this to the competent authorities in order for the perpetrators of all this to be prosecuted"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, in this report he does not need to mention that, but he did. He said a name and surname, and it's quite certain that he had to set this into motion -- or, rather, to report this. I don't know about Sapina, but I think Vlatko Rajic was a mentally disturbed person. I don't know about this other man, Sapina. But I learnt about this case later on, I think, or at this Tribunal. He ended up at the psychiatric ward as mentally disturbed, and he could not have been tried. But once you name names and mention events, which Mr. Siljeg does very properly, then of course the next step would be -- the next thing would be -- well, otherwise he'd skip the names and skip the event. And as a well-trained policeman from before, how would he not report this to the military investigators to deal with the person who was the perpetrator? As far as I can see, Siljeg has not hidden anything here. Everything he learnt and everything that he observed is noted here. Of course, an investigation then begins to protect a certain area, to take statements and so on. The procedure that we've discussed here was unleashed, and we looked into who should have done what and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. It seems that after the combat there were 132 members of the ABiH captured by the HVO, and 23 members of HVO were captured by the ABiH. As far as you know, the 23 prisoners, HVO prisoners, were they eventually exchanged? What happened to them? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I was able to see at this Tribunal and some documents, it was an exchange all for all, on an all-for-all basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's ten minutes left, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my colleague will allow me for the record to help everybody out, this man mentioned, Vlatko Rajic, now, three documents have been admitted into evidence about the fact that this man Vlatko Rajic was prosecuted. I can -- yes, I see him nodding. It is 2D008899 [as interpreted]. I think that is the judgement. Then there's another court document from those proceedings which is 1D00946. Those are the relevant documents and numbers. And there's another one which I think is a certificate on the sentence served, and it is 1D00945. The first number is 2D00889. Thank you. I repeated that first number. So I hope I have been of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It may be helpful for the purposes of the understandability of the record that we recall the crime committed by this Mr. Rajic. I think it was the murder of a young girl early in the morning when the family was told to move from the house. Is that correct? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The event was in Vakuf, and a throat was slit, a young man's throat was slit, head cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I mixed it up with another case where also the perpetrator had been prosecuted, and also he was a psychiatric case and dealt with by psychiatric treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. Stringer. But that was Ante Bunoza, and it concerned Capljina, and it was the killing of that girl. Her name was Kaplan, and he was sentenced to prison term of five years but he didn't undergo psychiatric treatment. He did, in fact, spend time in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my intention is to round off the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in the next six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, say that you would prefer to start tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. Actually, I was trying to make a joke, Judge Trechsel, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We'd never have guessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I could ask a few preliminary questions maybe to set the stage for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Can we agree that very early in January of 1993, Mate Boban, on behalf of the Bosnian Croat side, signed off on all of the components of the plan? Agreed to it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, as it existed in January of 1993, consisted of different parts, different annexes? There was a part on the constitutional framework. There was the proposed map with the cantons. There was a cease-fire agreement. There were various components of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Is that correct, based on what you know -- on what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I knew that there were constitutional frameworks, that they had proposed maps, corridors linking up certain provinces or cantons, and that there was an agreement about moving out the heavy weapons and so on and so forth. But the constitutional solutions to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was certainly there, and the maps were proposed for the territorial set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina internally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me if I suggested to you that on the 10th of January, 1993, Alija Izetbegovic signed off on the constitutional framework part of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did sign the constitutional part, and I think -- well, I don't know for sure, but I think he also signed up to the separation and delineation with some examples, the corridor through Posavina, and he had some other objections and provisos and asked the international community to prevail upon the Serb side to sign too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that on the 10th of January he did not sign off on or agree to the proposed map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he lay down certain conditions, but I can't say with certainty. I think he signed conditionally. He signed and then wanted to have it fine-tuned during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll get to this probably tomorrow. I think that on the conditions you might be referring possibly to events in March of 1993. Maybe just in the very little time that's left, let me just read from one of the exhibits and we'll see if we can agree as to what was the situation on the 10th of January. This is P01187, and, General, I don't think we have this translated into Croatian. It's among those UN-type documents that we don't have to have translations for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, am I correct in assuming that you are now turning to another binder --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- which is not distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge. It's in the binder that we've been working on. It's just earlier. P01187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I skipped over this earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer. I apologise. Since you spoke about the binders, I wonder if I may ask you to give us instructions. Which binders should we carry and take to them my office and then it bring it to tomorrow to conference room 1, because I believe that is why we have -- we have to remove -- I believe that list 6 and 7, but you may tell us otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Judge Prandler, since we're really at the end of the day, we are binder number 7, which is the binder we've been in, and I can inform everyone what the exhibits are going to be on this so that they can look at them tonight if they want. It's P01187, which actually we do have a translation into Croatian. And then P09852. Those two exhibits are in binder number 7, which we have -- or which everyone already has. So those are the only two documents that we're going to be using to talk about Vance-Owen. Probably also we'll go to Presidential Transcript, P01158, which is also in binder 7. And then after that we'll be finished with binder 7 and we'll go to binder 8, which we'll be distributing before court tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you've understood, for some kind of reason, some undetermined reason, we're moved to Courtroom I. Gotovina case is going to sit in Courtroom III. Sometimes they sat in Courtroom II, and II is free tomorrow, but they're moving to III. I don't know what Registry did but if they knew the amount of binders we have to move with us, they probably wouldn't have told us to go to Courtroom I. But Judges, we'll take binder number 7, and we'll leave the courtroom with this binder to make sure that our assistants don't have to do this work of lugging volumes and volumes of documents all around the Tribunal. And tomorrow we'll have the great pleasure of inaugurating binder number 8, but it will be in Courtroom I. So tomorrow we meet at 9.00, Courtroom I. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
